Seignanx XV · U16 · Season 2026-2027

Our key principles of play

“A player who understands why he does things will be better able to make the right choices.”

Attack (us)DefenceThe animations loop: watch them several times.
PassingSupport1 v 1 ZonesKick-offsKicking ExitsScoring zoneSet piecesFrench callsDefence
Attack

Passing: flat or deep

Flat

The attackers are in a line, close to the defence. The receiver takes the ball at speed, on the line.

Goal: break the line. The defender has no time to recover.

Deep

The attackers are in a staircase, further from the defence.

Goal: get time to read the defence and send the ball where there is space.

Why?

A defence that rushes up smothers a flat attack: then we need depth. A defence that waits gives us time to attack flat, and that is where we break the line.

Attack

Support: the -1 and the +1

  • The -1 is the player who has just passed. He does not stop: he offers an option in line with, or slightly inside, the ball carrier who is taking on his defender.
  • The +1 is on the outside. He closes in on the ball carrier.
Why?

The ball carrier must never be alone. With a -1 and a +1 close by, he always has an option: an offload, or a quick ruck because the support arrives first.

Attack

1 v 1, with and without the ball

Without the ball: where do I stand?

The +1 calls for the ball and moves into the free space:

  • Defenders spread out: I come close to the ball carrier, cutting back into the gap.
  • Defenders tight together: I stay far away, out wide, where they are not.

With the ball: winning my 1 v 1

  • I run at my defender to fix him.
  • I stay dynamic with quick feet to work him.
  • I attack his weak shoulder.
  • I have won the duel when I am past the defenders' shoulder line.
Why?

A defender on his heels cannot tackle hard. Once I am past his shoulders, even if I am tackled, I go forward: the ball comes back quickly and the defence goes backwards.

Reading the pitch

The pitch in three zones

ZoneWhere?What we want
1From our try line to our 30 mGet out of our half without taking risks (see “Exits”).
2From our 30 m to 10 m from their try lineCreate: this is where we play our moves. If a move does not create an overlap, we can finish it with a kick.
3The last 10 metres before their try lineScore: keep the ball, tap penalties, scoring moves.

Moves depending on the scrum

In zone 2, where the scrum is across the pitch decides the move. All our moves are explained, with animations, in the slides: Backline moves 2026-2027.

ScrumMove
In the middleBrive: the 9 fakes an 8-9, the 10 comes back to attack the open side
Brive minus: the 10 makes the same run, but the 8 passes to the 9 on the other side, who then plays with the 15
15-20 m from the left touchlineTarbes: the 8 attacks the 10's area, two phases in the same direction, then switch
15-20 m from the left or right touchlineSeignanx: the 12 crashes in, the 13 cuts back, the 10 runs behind (3 options)
Pivot 13: miss pass to the 13, pivot and inside pass
S13: the 10 runs straight, planned scissors with the 12
From a lineoutTortue (Turtle). Pivot 13, S13 and Seignanx can also be played from a lineout
Why?

We do not take the same risks 10 m from our try line and 10 m from theirs. Knowing which zone you are in tells you what to do with the ball.

Restarts

Kick-offs

Receiving the kick-off

The forwards stand in two matching groups of three, with the hooker and the 8 in the middle:

  • The prop just behind the point where the 10 m line (our 40 m) meets the 15 m line.
  • The lock in the 5 m channel, a little behind the prop.
  • The flanker between the two, but in front of our 22 m.
  • The other forwards do the same on the other side. The hooker and the 8 in the middle.
Why?

The pitch is covered in width and depth: a short kick-off lands on a prop, a long one on a flanker, and each group of three is ready to support the catcher.

Our kick-off

  • Everyone starts behind the kicker, in one line.
  • The fastest players and the jumpers contest the ball as it comes down.
  • The others form a curtain to tackle the catcher as fast as possible.
Strategy

Kicking

Why kick?

  • Gain ground when going forward with the ball in hand costs too much.
  • Win the ball back by putting pressure on the catcher.
  • Get out of our half (zone 1).
  • Play behind a defence that rushes up.

The different kicks

KickWho?What for?
Box kick behind the forwardsThe 9Win the ball back, exit
High contestable kickThe 10Win the ball back going forward
Long territorial kickThe 10, the 15Gain ground
Kick to touchThe 10, the 15Exit, gain ground safely
Chip, grubber, cross-kickThe 10, the backsPlay behind a rushing defence, in the scoring zone

When to kick?

  • When the ball is slow and the defenders are set in a line: we go forward with the boot. The 9 kicks high to win it back, or the 10 kicks to gain ground.
  • We can finish a move with a kick if it has not created an overlap.
Why?

A kick is a pass to the whole team: it is only worth something if everyone chases, in a line, behind the kicker.

Zone 1

Exits

  • Who? The 9, the 10 or the 15.
  • The 9 kicks from behind his forwards.
  • The 10 kicks to the nearest touchline, the British way.
  • After a scrum in the middle: first one phase (like Seignanx option 2) to get closer to a touchline, then the kick.

Depending on the opposition

A team that loves to counter-attack

We kick the ball into the stands, to touch. We give them no counter-attack ball.

A team that is very strong at the lineout

We keep the ball in play with long kicks, and we come up together in defence.

Why?

From the middle, the touchline is too far for a safe kick. One phase towards one side brings the touchline closer and gives the 10 time and a better angle to kick.

Zone 3

The scoring zone

Tap penalty: specials 1, 2 and 3. We play twice in the same direction with forwards bound together before contact, then we switch play with speed.

Why?

Forwards bound before contact go forward and keep the ball. Two phases in the same direction force the defence to slide: on the other side there are fewer defenders, and a fast switch catches them before they get back.

Set pieces

Set pieces: lineout and scrum

Our lineout

All our lineout calls, with animations, are in the slides: Lineouts 2026-2027.

  • The receiver is the 9, except when the next phase is a maul or a dummy maul: then it is the 5.

Defending a 5-man lineout: two options

Option 1: half-pod + pod of 3

At the front, a half-pod: one jumper lifted by one prop. Behind, a pod of 3.

The two pods stand close together: their hooker has to throw over the top or force his throw.

Option 2: the pivot prop

A pivot prop lifts either the first pod or the second pod.

The opposition does not know where we will jump.

Defending a full lineout

  • We put up two pods standing very close together.
The clue

Watch their back lifter: if he bends his legs hard, there is a good chance they will jump there.

The receiver when defending a lineout

  • Usually, the 2 is the receiver: he must read it early if the pod is beaten by a lob. The 9 is in the tramlines.
  • In our 22 m, it is the other way round: the 2 in the tramlines, the 9 as receiver. Near our line, opponents often have moves to attack the tramlines.

Defending a scrum

  • The flankers stay alert to defend against breaks by the 8 and the 9.
  • If the 9 passes to the backs, the flanker is on a mission: he comes up and keeps going until the tackle.
Why?

Set pieces give the first ball. In defence at the lineout, disrupting their throw or their jump takes away their move. At the scrum, a flanker who keeps going adds one more defender in the backline.

Backline moves

Useful words

Defence

Defence

  • The basis is communication. Everyone calls the player he is taking.
  • I stand on the inside of the player I am marking, which means on the side the ball is coming from. Never let him get on your inside.
  • I come up and line up my opponent.
  • If my player passes, I keep going until the tackle.
  • If possible, the -1 competes for the ball on the ground.
  • If the opposition secure the ball well, we do not commit: players move across. How many depends on the width left on each side.
  • We come up on both sides of the ruck to stop them switching play.

Depending on numbers

When we are outnumbered

The rule: do not get beaten. We control the ball carrier and slide: we push him towards the touchline.

The picture: a curtain being drawn.

When the numbers are equal

We come up hard, together.

The picture: a wall moving forward.

The tackle

  1. Same leg, same shoulder: I tackle with my right shoulder with my right leg forward, and the other way round.
  2. Hit hard with the shoulder, driving off the front leg.
  3. I drive through the ball carrier as if I want to go through him.
  4. My arms pull the opponent's legs towards me to knock him off balance.
  5. Head up and clear, eyes on his hips.
Why?

A line that talks and comes up together leaves no gaps. Defending from the inside pushes the attack towards the touchline, where it has less space. Coming up on both sides of the ruck shuts down the switch.
